title: Apple Sauce
subtitle: Sharp Bramley purée, the classic pork companion
excerpt: Two ingredients, ten minutes: Bramley apples cooked to a soft, sharp purée with a little butter and sugar. The essential accompaniment to roast pork, sausages, and pork chops.

recipe.sourceNotes: Apple sauce as a companion to pork has deep roots in British cooking, appearing in recipe collections from the seventeenth century. The combination made practical sense: pigs were often raised on apple orchards in the west of England, particularly in Somerset, Herefordshire, and Gloucestershire, and the acidity of the apple cuts through the richness of pork fat in a way that is both refreshing and digestively useful. The Bramley Seedling, the dominant British cooking apple, was discovered in Nottinghamshire in the early nineteenth century and remains the standard for sauce because it collapses completely when cooked and has a pronounced tartness. Apple sauce is also served with roast goose and duck in the Christmas tradition.

content.text: Use Bramley apples: they collapse to a fluffy purée without any stirring or blending. Eating apples hold their shape and need to be crushed, producing a chunkier result with less natural tartness. The amount of sugar needed depends entirely on how sharp the apples are; start with less and adjust once the apples have softened.

Put the apple, butter, and 1 tablespoon of sugar in a small saucepan with 2 tablespoons of water. Cover and cook over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the apple has completely collapsed into a purée.

Remove from the heat. If the sauce is lumpy, beat it with a wooden spoon or pass it through a sieve. Taste and add more sugar if needed. Add a squeeze of lemon juice for a sharper result. Serve warm or at room temperature.
